blocks.text: The distinctive feature of medical education is how completely theoretical and scientific knowledge is fused with the results derived from experience. It must be remembered that the clinical teacher has an inmediate reponsibility to his patients as well as to his students. This double load of theory and practice is particularly heavier when great advances are being made in medical science.

In most countries students must complete a four-or five-year medical education in order to obtain the license to practice. After that, in the present conditions, a practitioner of any branch of medicine needs at least four years to complete reasonably adequate training.

The premedical courses required in most countries are in the subjects of physics, chemistry and biology. Graduation from a recognized secondary school is required. Each of the courses should include laboratory periods of from two hours to six hours a week for a full academic year. However, the extent of the student’s familiarity with the use of instruments and laboratory procedures varies widely from country to country depending on the funds each country can use to support this expensive instruction.
The medical schools begin their work with the study of the structure of the body and its formation: anatomy, histology and embryology.

The sequence of the courses and the emphasis the schools give certain areas may differ from country to country, but medical schools should by all means adhere to the following basic pursuits: superior quality of the teaching staff, a high ratio of teaching staff to students, and adequate funds for laboratory work and research.

items: *Mr. Harris:* Hi, honey. I’m back from work.
*Cindy:* Hi, darling. What’s wrong with you? You look so pale and tired.
*Mr. Harris:* Oh, I don’t know. About two hours ago I began to feel awful. I’ve got awful pains in my belly.
*Cindy:* You have to see a doctor at once. Let me take you to the hospital.
*Dr. Kramer:* Hello, I’m Dr. Kramer. What seems to be the trouble? What brings you to the emergency room?
*Mr. Harris:* It’s this awful pain in my belly.
*Dr. Kramer:* When did this pain start?
*Mr. Harris:* This morning. Up here, but now it’s here, and it really hurts.
*Dr. Kramer:* How was it this morning?
*Mr. Harris:* Well, it wasn’t really very bad. The pain came and went, and I did some work in my office, but now I can’t stand it any more. It’s killing me.
*Dr. Kramer:* Have you lost your appetite?
*Mr. Harris:* Oh, sure. I haven’t had anything to eat since yesterday evening. I couldn’t even look at or smell food.
*Dr. Kramer:* Have you had any bowel movements?
*Mr. Harris:* Not for two days.
*Dr. Kramer:* Would you say this is normal?
*Mr. Harris:* No, as a rule I have one every day.
*Dr. Kramer:* Any diarrhea?
*Mr. Harris:* No.
*Dr. Kramer:* How about nausea and vomiting?
*Mr. Harris:* Last night it was really bad. I was vomiting about every two hours. It’s a little better now. Oh, oh, it’s coming again.
*Dr. Kramer:* Nurse, please help us. This seems to be a case of appendicitis.
